relevance_reason: The paper describes a patient with a progressive mild-variant EMARDD (mvEMARDD) phenotype who carries a novel homozygous MEGF10 missense variant.

findings.statement: Croci et al. (2022) reported a 22-year-old Italian man, born to healthy consanguineous parents, who had a congenital myopathic phenotype with weak suction, elbow contractures and scoliosis from the first months of life. He was born at 33 weeks' gestation and needed resuscitation for asphyxia. Motor development and intellect were normal. He then developed slowly progressive muscle weakness with impaired walking, rhinolalia, dysphagia and respiratory involvement, and needed nocturnal noninvasive ventilation from age 16 years. On examination he had axial hypotonia, generalized muscle hypotrophy, cleft palate, global areflexia, contractures of the elbows and ankles, and hyperlordosis. Serum CK, brain and spine MRI, and cardiac studies were normal.
quotes: He had weak suction and presented with a congenital myopathic phenotype with elbow contractures and scoliosis since the first months of life.

No motor developmental delay or intellectual disability were observed, but he developed a slowly progressive muscle weakness with impaired walking, rhinolalia, dysphagia, and respiratory involvement, which required nocturnal non-invasive ventilation therapy since the age of 16 years.
Follow-up neurological examination showed axial hypotonia, generalised muscular hypotrophy and weakness (Fig. 2), preserved facial expressions, cleft palate, and global areflexia.

findings.statement: Croci et al. (2022) found that the patient's first muscle biopsy, taken at age 5 years, showed nonspecific changes: variation in fiber size, internal nuclei and fibrosis. A later biopsy showed myofibrillar alterations, including whorled fibers, cytoplasmic inclusions and minicores. Electrophysiologic studies were normal apart from reduced amplitude of the muscle evoked potential. The authors proposed that the minicores seen in the late-onset group may result from longstanding myofibrillar pathology that begins in infancy.
quotes: A first muscle biopsy at age of 5 years, revealed unspecific muscle damage, with fibre size variation, internal nuclei and fibrosis. In a second muscle biopsy performed years later, myofibrillar alterations were noted, including whorled fibres, cytoplasmic inclusion and minicores (Fig. 1).
Thus, we propose that minicores that mark the late onset group, can actually be a consequence of a longstanding myofibrillar pathological processes starting in infancy.

phenotypes.hpo_label: Increased variability in muscle fiber diameter

findings.statement: In an Italian man with a progressive form of mvEMARDD, Croci et al. (2022) used exome sequencing to identify a homozygous missense variant in the MEGF10 gene, c.2096G-C (p.Cys699Ser; NM_001256545.2). Sanger sequencing confirmed the variant, and both consanguineous parents were heterozygous carriers. The variant was absent from ClinVar and gnomAD, changes a conserved cysteine in an EGF-like domain, and was predicted to be damaging by in silico tools. It was classified as likely pathogenic.
quotes: Exome sequencing led to the identification of the homozygous variant (NM_001256545.2): c.2096G > C (p.Cys699Ser) in the MEGF10 gene. This variant is absent in genomic databases (such as ClinVar and gnomAD), affects a conserved residue (GERP score = 5.85)
Sanger sequencing was also performed and confirmed that the patient was homozygous for the variant, and both parents were carriers.
In our patient, we identified the novel homozygous variant p.Cys699S affecting a very conserved cysteine residue in a crucial EGF-like functional domain.

findings.statement: Croci et al. (2022) noted that missense variants in MEGF10 have been associated with later onset and a milder course. Their patient carried a missense variant but had early-onset myopathy with a progressive course. The authors proposed that MEGF10-related phenotypes form a continuum rather than a dichotomy between classic EMARDD and mvEMARDD.
quotes: Although our patient carried a missense variant, he displayed an early-onset myopathy with progressive course.

In summary, our report proposes a continuum in the phenotypes associated with MEGF10 variants, which include a clinical and histopathological progression of the disease and represent a novelty from the dichotomy between the early onset classic severe EMARDD and mvEMARDD.

relevance_reason: Reports a Japanese patient with the milder MEGF10 myopathy phenotype carrying compound heterozygous variants, including a novel cysteine missense variant, which bears on the genotype-phenotype correlation for CMYO10B.

findings.statement: Takayama et al. (2016) reported a Japanese patient with the milder phenotype of MEGF10 myopathy who carried compound heterozygous MEGF10 mutations: a splice site mutation (c.2981-2A>G) and a novel missense mutation (p.Cys810Tyr).
quotes: the other with the milder phenotype who harbored a compound heterozygous mutation, c.2981-2A > G, and a novel missense mutation, p.Cys810Tyr

findings.statement: Takayama et al. (2016) noted that cysteine mutations in the extracellular EGF-like domain of MEGF10 may be responsible for the milder phenotype. They reported 2 Japanese patients: one with the severe EMARDD phenotype who had a novel homozygous frameshift mutation (c.131_132del), and one with the milder phenotype who had a compound heterozygous mutation that included the cysteine missense mutation p.Cys810Tyr. The authors concluded that these findings indicated a genotype-phenotype correlation in MEGF10 myopathy.
quotes: Cysteine mutations in the extracellular EGF-like domain may be responsible for the milder phenotype, but the relationship is not conclusive because of the few reports of this disorder.
one with EMARDD phenotype who had a novel homozygous frameshift mutation, c.131_132del
This is the first report on East Asian patients with MEGF10 myopathy showing two phenotypes, indicating the genotype-phenotype correlation in MEGF10 myopathy.

findings.statement: Takayama et al. (2016) stated that mutations in MEGF10 cause early-onset myopathy with areflexia, respiratory distress, and dysphagia (EMARDD) as well as a milder phenotype of minicore myopathy. At the time of their report, 6 families with EMARDD and 1 with the milder disorder had been described.
quotes: Mutations in the multiple epidermal growth factor-like domains 10 (MEGF10: NM_032446.2) gene are known to cause early-onset myopathy characterized by areflexia, respiratory distress, and dysphagia (EMARDD: OMIM 614399), and a milder phenotype of minicore myopathy.
To date, there have been reports of six families with EMARDD and one with a milder disorder.

relevance_reason: Reports a patient with adult-onset mild MEGF10 myopathy carrying a novel p.G739R variant and a genotype-phenotype analysis showing missense alleles are associated with later onset.

findings.statement: Fujii et al. (2022) reported a man with progressive weakness that began in his thirties, who developed severe respiratory failure at age 66 years. His muscle biopsy showed no clear cores.
quotes: We present a patient who had progressive weakness since his 30 s and then developed severe respiratory failure at the age of 66 years
He had no clear core in the biopsied muscle.

phenotypes.hpo_label: Type 1 and type 2 muscle fiber minicore regions

findings.statement: In a man with adult-onset progressive myopathy and respiratory failure, Fujii et al. (2022) identified a novel mutation, p.G739R, in the MEGF10 gene.
quotes: found that he had a novel mutation, p.G739R, in MEGF10

findings.statement: Fujii et al. (2022) summarized their patient and previously reported patients with MEGF10 mutations and found that patients with missense mutations in at least 1 allele had significantly later onset than those with biallelic truncating mutations. They noted that some reported patients with the mild variant phenotype had no clear cores.
quotes: Results show that patients with missense mutations in at least one allele had significantly later onset than those with biallelic truncation mutations.
Recently, a mild variant phenotype of EMARDD has been reported in patients with multiple minicores in the myofibers. However, some reported patients had no clear cores.

relevance_reason: The paper reports an adult-onset patient with compound heterozygous MEGF10 variants, which is a mild-variant phenotype, and reviews genotype-phenotype correlation across reported cases.

findings.statement: Harris et al. (2018) reported a 66-year-old man with a 20-year history of progressive proximal and distal weakness of the upper and lower limbs, facial weakness, and dysphagia. In his 50s, while still ambulant, he developed respiratory failure that required ventilation. Muscle biopsy showed myopathic changes with aggregation of myofibrillar proteins.
quotes: We undertook exome sequencing in a 66 year old male with a 20 year history of progressive proximal and distal weakness of upper and lower limbs, facial weakness and dysphagia, who developed respiratory failure requiring ventilation while still ambulant in his 50s.
Muscle biopsy demonstrated myopathic changes with aggregation of myofibrillar proteins.

findings.statement: In a 66-year-old man with adult-onset MEGF10-related myopathy, Harris et al. (2018) used exome sequencing to identify a novel essential splice-site variant in the MEGF10 gene (c.1426+1G>T). The variant was described in the context of recessive MEGF10 mutations.
quotes: Mutations in MEGF10 were identified: a novel essential splice site (c.1426+1G>T) and a novel missense variant (c.352T>C, p.(Cys118Arg)).

findings.statement: In the same patient, Harris et al. (2018) identified by exome sequencing a novel missense variant in the MEGF10 gene, c.352T>C (p.Cys118Arg), which was the second mutation found alongside the c.1426+1G>T splice-site variant.
quotes: Mutations in MEGF10 were identified: a novel essential splice site (c.1426+1G>T) and a novel missense variant (c.352T>C, p.(Cys118Arg)).

findings.statement: Harris et al. (2018) reviewed all 20 reported cases with MEGF10 mutations and confirmed a genotype-phenotype correlation. In patients with at least 1 null mutation, respiratory dysfunction began in the first year of life. In patients with 2 missense mutations, respiratory dysfunction began at about 10 years of age or much later. The authors stated that their findings expanded the phenotype to include onset in the fifth decade.
quotes: We performed a detailed review of all reported MEGF10 cases (n = 20), and confirmed the presence of a genotype-phenotype correlation, namely that with ≥1 null mutation onset of respiratory dysfunction occurs in the first year of life, whereas with 2 missense mutations, respiratory dysfunction occurs at 10 years old or much later
Our findings expand the phenotype of MEGF10 mutations to include onset in the 5th decade

relevance_reason: The paper reports the family that defines the mild MEGF10 congenital myopathy with minicores: compound heterozygous missense mutations, a clinical and pathology description, and zebrafish knockdown results.

findings.statement: Boyden et al. (2012) reported a nonconsanguineous Caucasian family of mixed European ancestry (family 1030) in which 3 of 4 sibs had an autosomal recessive myopathy that resembled multiminicore disease. Weakness began by 12 months of age, first in the neck. It was mainly axial and proximal, included facial weakness, and stabilized in adolescence. Neck contractures appeared in infancy, and elbow, knee, and heel-cord contractures developed by adulthood. Serum CK was mildly elevated. All 3 patients had childhood-onset scoliosis treated with spinal fusion, and from age 10 to 11 years all had respiratory problems requiring nighttime bilevel positive airway pressure. All 3 had hypernasal speech; 1 was born with a cleft palate and another had a midline palatal ridge.
quotes: Affected members of family 1030 presented with weakness by 12 months of age, initially in the neck. Weakness was present throughout the body but was primarily axial and proximal and stabilized in adolescence. Facial weakness was also evident.

All three patients had childhood onset scoliosis and were treated with spinal fusion surgery, and beginning at age 10–11 years, they all developed respiratory problems treated with bilevel positive airway pressure ventilation at night.

One of the patients had cleft palate at birth that was surgically repaired, and a second had a midline ridge on her palate in adulthood, while the palate of the third patient appeared normal. All three affected siblings had hypernasal speech

findings.statement: Boyden et al. (2012) found that muscle biopsies from family 1030 showed dystrophic features: fatty replacement of myofibers, increased perimysial and endomysial connective tissue, and isolated regenerating fibers. They also showed myopathic features, namely moth-eaten fibers and minicores, the minicores mainly in type I fibers. Rimmed vacuoles, inclusions, central cores, nemaline rods, and ragged red fibers were absent. Type I fibers slightly predominated and varied more in size than type II fibers.
quotes: Muscle biopsy tissue from affected subjects showed replacement of myofibers with fatty tissue, increased perimysial and endomysial connective tissue, and isolated regenerating fibers, features found in muscular dystrophies (Fig. 2). However, moth-eaten fibers and minicores were also observed, suggestive of a congenital myopathy.
Rimmed vacuoles, inclusions, central cores, nemaline rods, and ragged red fibers were absent.
Overall, there was a slight predominance of type I fibers, and they showed a more pronounced variability in size than type II fibers.

phenotypes.hpo_label: Central core regions in muscle fibers

findings.statement: Boyden et al. (2012) carried out a genomewide linkage scan in family 1030 that gave positive LOD scores at 16 loci. MEGF10 lay within a linkage peak on chromosome 5 that reached the maximum possible LOD score of 1.329. The analysis excluded SEPN1, RYR1, ACTA1, and TPM3.
quotes: MEGF10 lies within a linkage peak on chromosome 5 that reached the maximum possible LOD score of 1.329.
Both SEPN1 and RYR1 were excluded, as were ACTA1 and TPM3

findings.statement: Boyden et al. (2012) combined whole genome sequencing with linkage data and found that affected members of family 1030 were compound heterozygous for 2 missense mutations in MEGF10, c.976T-C (p.C326R) in exon 10 and c.2320T-C (p.C774R) in exon 19. The mutations were in trans and segregated with the disease in all 6 family members. Both were absent from dbSNP, 1000 Genomes, and the Exome Sequencing Project, and from 715 and 645 genotyped controls, respectively. Each mutation replaces a cysteine that is conserved in 43 of 43 species, in EGF-like domains 6 and 16, and the authors predicted that this disrupts disulfide bonds.
quotes: the heterozygous missense mutations c.976T > C (p.C326R) and c.2320T > C (p.C774R) in MEGF10, the sole remaining candidate, were confirmed by Sanger sequencing to be in trans in affected subjects and to segregate with the myopathy in all six family members.
The c.976T > C and c.2320T > C mutations were also absent from 715 and 645 genotyped unaffected control subjects, respectively (Table 1).
The p.C326R and p.C774R mutations substitute the fourth and sixth cysteines of EGF-like domains six and sixteen, respectively, for arginines.

findings.statement: Boyden et al. (2012) described a sporadic female patient (105-1) of Caucasian origin with distant Portuguese ancestry who had been diagnosed with multiminicore disease. She had hypotonia at several weeks of age, a markedly high-arched palate, failure to thrive from poor feeding, blue sclerae, and hyperflexible joints. In childhood she had frequent pulmonary infections but no chronic breathing problems. At age 10 years her serum CK was 302 U/L. Her scoliosis reached 20 degrees by age 12, and she had mild, nonprogressive proximal and facial weakness. Muscle biopsy showed minicores, which electron microscopy confirmed.
quotes: At several weeks of age, she presented with hypotonia, initially manifesting as a weak neck and floppy head. A markedly high arched palate and failure to thrive as a result of poor feeding were noted, as were blue-tinged sclera and hyperflexible joints.
Serum CK level at age 10 years was mildly elevated at 302 U/L (upper limit of reference range 105 U/L), and mild scoliosis was reported at the same time, which progressed to 20° by age 12 years.
Electron microscopy showed focal areas of Z-band disarray devoid of mitochondria and extending across a few sarcomeres in the longitudinal axis, confirming the presence of minicores.

phenotypes.text: failure to thrive due to poor feeding

findings.statement: Boyden et al. (2012) sequenced MEGF10 in 190 patients with unexplained myopathies and found 1 patient (105-1) with a single heterozygous mutation, c.211C-T (p.R71W), in the emilin domain. The variant was absent from public databases and from 699 controls, and it was inherited from an unaffected parent. Sequencing of muscle cDNA did not reveal a second mutation. Because the patient's clinical and histologic features resembled those of family 1030, the authors suggested she may carry a second MEGF10 mutation they could not detect.
quotes: subject 105-1 carried a novel c.211C > T (p.R71W) mutation that was absent from dbSNP v135, 1,000 Genomes data, ESP data, 56 internal genomes, and 699 genotyped unaffected control subjects.
The c.211C > T mutation was heterozygous in an unaffected parent of subject 105-1, so it was not de novo dominant.
subject 105-1 may carry a second mutation in MEGF10 that we were unable to detect.

findings.statement: Boyden et al. (2012) observed that patients with MEGF10 missense mutations had a phenotype similar to, but milder than, the severe congenital myopathy previously reported with nonsense and frameshift mutations. They attributed this to residual MEGF10 function in their patients, in contrast to total loss of expression in the earlier families. Minicores were prominent in their missense-mutation patients but had not been noted in the families with null mutations.
quotes: The phenotypes described therein are generally similar to those of families 1030 and 105, but are more severe.
Accordingly, affected members of family 1030 may retain a small amount of residual MEGF10 function
minicores were not noted in the biopsies from the reported families with null mutations but were a prominent feature in our patients with missense mutations.

findings.statement: Boyden et al. (2012) knocked down megf10 in zebrafish with 4 different splice-blocking morpholinos. The morphants had curled or bent tails, impaired swimming, reduced response to touch, and unhatched eggs. They also showed reduced birefringence, disrupted somite boundaries, gaps between myofibers, and myofibrillar disorganization on electron microscopy, which the authors took as consistent with a myopathic process.
quotes: Anti-megf10 morpholinos resulted in several phenotypes at 4 days post-fertilization, generally including curled or bent tails, impaired swimming behavior, and diminished motility in response to touch, all consistent with a myopathy
MO2-treated zebrafish muscle showed widespread myofibrillar disorganization and decreased striation (Online Resource 15).

findings.statement: Boyden et al. (2012) hypothesized that loss of MEGF10 function causes satellite cells to differentiate excessively, depleting the self-renewing cells that regenerate damaged muscle fibers. They suggested that satellite cell dysfunction could be a pathogenic mechanism shared with SEPN1-related multiminicore disease.
quotes: we hypothesize that excessive differentiation of satellite cells could deplete the population of self-renewing cells available to regenerate damaged muscle fibers.
may arise through a common pathogenic mechanism of satellite cell dysfunction.

relevance_reason: Reports two sisters with an adult-onset mild MEGF10 myopathy with minicores and novel compound heterozygous MEGF10 variants.

findings.statement: Liewluck et al. (2016) reported 2 sisters who had respiratory insufficiency beginning in adulthood, followed later by limb weakness. Both sisters had scoliosis, hyperlaxity of the distal joints, and high-arched feet. A right triceps muscle biopsy from one sister showed multiple minicores, and her EMG showed myopathic changes with fibrillation potentials and myotonic discharges.
quotes: We report 2 sisters with adult-onset respiratory insufficiency followed by development of limb weakness. Both had scoliosis, distal joint hyperlaxity, and high-arched feet.
A biopsy of the right triceps muscle in 1 sister showed multiple minicore structures. She had electromyographic changes of myopathy with fibrillation potentials and myotonic discharges.

phenotypes.hpo_label: Type 1 and type 2 muscle fiber minicore regions

findings.statement: In 2 sisters with adult-onset myopathy with minicores, respiratory insufficiency, and scoliosis, Liewluck et al. (2016) used next-generation sequencing to identify compound heterozygous missense variants in the MEGF10 gene: c.230G>A (p.Arg77Gln) and c.1833T>G (p.Cys611Trp). The authors concluded that MEGF10 mutations can cause myopathy with respiratory insufficiency beginning in adulthood.
quotes: Next generation sequencing identified novel compound heterozygous missense variants in MEGF10 c.230G>A (p.Arg77Gln) and c.1833T>G (p.Cys611Trp) in both sisters.
MEGF10 mutations can cause myopathy with adult-onset respiratory insufficiency.

relevance_reason: The paper describes a Saudi boy with a mild, ambulant form of MEGF10-related congenital myopathy caused by a homozygous splice-site variant, with RT-PCR evidence of an aberrant transcript. It contrasts him with a second, severely affected patient.

findings.statement: AlMuhaizea et al. (2021) reported a boy (patient 2) from a consanguineous Saudi family (parents were first cousins) with a mild form of MEGF10-related congenital myopathy. He had generalized hypotonia from the newborn period, after a pregnancy with decreased fetal movements. He had feeding difficulties, choking, recurrent aspiration pneumonia and motor delay, but he sat at 21 months and was walking independently, though running slowly, at age 9 years. He had no major cognitive deficits and did not need long-term oxygen. On examination he had plagiocephaly, facial diplegia, a high-arched palate, low-set ears, mild thoracic scoliosis with spinal rigidity, axial-predominant hypotonia, proximal weakness, a positive Gowers sign, areflexia and joint hyperlaxity. Creatine kinase was normal, nerve conduction was normal, EMG showed neurogenic changes, and a modified barium study showed mild oral dysphagia. A sister with a similar phenotype died at 18 months of respiratory infections.
quotes: A four-year-old boy from a consanguineous Saudi family (first-degree cousins) presented with neonatal-onset generalized hypotonia. The pregnancy was complicated by decreased fetal movements. He had one sister with a similar phenotype who passed away at the age of 18 months with respiratory infections.

His last clinical follow up was at the age of 9 years when he was noted to be walking independently, but was a slow runner. He was able to draw a line and completely undress himself. He engaged in-group play and had no major cognitive deficits. He did not require long-term oxygen support.
He had a positive Gower sign but no calf muscle hypertrophy. His deep tendon reflexes were absent. He also had joint hyperlaxity of knees, wrists, and elbows.

findings.statement: In patient 2, AlMuhaizea et al. (2021) used a muscular dystrophy and myopathy gene panel and found a homozygous splice-site variant in the MEGF10 gene (c.2980+5G>C, NM_032446.2). Sanger sequencing confirmed it. RT-PCR on RNA from the patient's lymphoblastoid cells showed a larger, aberrant transcript, and sequencing showed that it retained 85 bp of intron 23. The panel also found a heterozygous PRKAG3 variant (c.364dupA, p.Thr122Asnfs*11).
quotes: For patient 2, comprehensive muscular dystrophy and myopathy gene panel revealed a splicing variant in MEGF10 (NM_032446.2:c.2980+5G>C:Exon21:Chr5:126784919)
Sanger sequencing analysis of the abnormal RT-PCR product showed retention of 85 bp from the intron 23, resulting in a larger aberrant transcript (Figure 4C).
In addition to this biallelic splice site variant, the panel revealed another pathogenic variant of PRKAG3 (c.364dupA, p.Thr122Asnfs*11) at heteroallelic state.

findings.statement: AlMuhaizea et al. (2021) also reported a severely affected boy (patient 1) from an unrelated consanguineous Saudi family. He had congenital hypotonia after a pregnancy with decreased fetal movements, and neonatal seizures that responded to phenobarbital. He had facial diplegia, ptosis, camptodactyly, pectus excavatum, scoliosis with butterfly vertebrae, right diaphragmatic eventration, developmental dysplasia of the hip, nephrolithiasis and absent tendon reflexes. He was never able to sit, needed gastrostomy feeding and supplemental oxygen, and had myopathic EMG changes. His muscle biopsy was essentially normal. He died at 8 months of respiratory failure, and an affected sister died at 11 months.
quotes: Unfortunately, the patient passed away at the age of eight months secondary to respiratory failure following a severe chest infection.
Spinal Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed scoliosis and right diaphragmatic eventration.
A skeletal muscle biopsy of the right thigh was essentially normal and showed minimal variation in myofiber size (Figure 2A) and unremarkable endomysial connective tissue.

findings.statement: In patient 1, who had the severe phenotype, AlMuhaizea et al. (2021) used a myopathy gene panel and found a homozygous frameshift variant in the MEGF10 gene (c.3132dupA, p.Glu1045Argfs*22, NM_032446.2).
quotes: A comprehensive myopathy gene panel for patient 1 revealed a homozygous variant in MEGF10 (NM_032446.2:c.3132dupA:p.Glu1045Argfs*22) (Figure 2D).

findings.statement: AlMuhaizea et al. (2021) noted that the 2 different MEGF10 variants were associated with different severity. The homozygous frameshift variant caused a severe phenotype with death in infancy. The homozygous splice-site variant caused a milder, ambulant phenotype resembling an axial-predominant myopathy with scoliosis and spinal rigidity.
quotes: Moreover, both variants lead to a different phenotypic onset of mild and severe types.

The 4-year-old boy presented with a milder phenotype. He is alive and his symptoms are milder, including dysphagia, scoliosis, and slower physical abilities compared to his peers. His phenotype is more of axial predominant myopathy with scoliosis and spine rigidity.

relevance_reason: Functional and animal model study of MEGF10 deficiency and the pathogenic p.C774R mutation in EMARDD; provides pathogenesis evidence relevant to MEGF10-related myopathy.

findings.statement: Saha et al. (2017) found that shRNA-mediated knockdown of Megf10, as well as overexpression of the pathogenic human MEGF10 p.C774R mutation, impaired proliferation and migration of C2C12 myoblasts.
quotes: We demonstrate that short hairpin RNA (shRNA)-mediated knockdown of Megf10, as well as overexpression of the pathogenic human p.C774R mutation, leads to impaired proliferation and migration of C2C12 cells.

findings.statement: Saha et al. (2017) showed by reciprocal coimmunoprecipitation that Megf10 and Notch1 interact via their respective intracellular domains, and that these interactions were impaired by the pathogenic p.C774R mutation. They suggested that Megf10 regulation of myoblast function is mediated at least in part via interactions with Notch signaling components, and that defects in these interactions may contribute to the pathogenesis of EMARDD.
quotes: Reciprocal co-immunoprecipitation studies show that Megf10 and Notch1 interact via their respective intracellular domains. These interactions are impaired by the pathogenic p.C774R mutation.
defects in these interactions may contribute to the pathogenesis of EMARDD

findings.statement: Saha et al. (2017) found that myoblasts from Megf10-null mice and Megf10/mdx double-knockout mice showed impaired proliferation and migration compared with myoblasts from wildtype and mdx mice, and that the double-knockout mice showed histologic abnormalities not observed in either single mutant mouse.
quotes: Myoblasts from Megf10-/- mice and Megf10-/-/mdx double knockout (dko) mice also show impaired proliferation and migration compared to myoblasts from wild type and mdx mice, whereas the dko mice show histological abnormalities that are not observed in either single mutant mouse.

relevance_reason: Mouse model study of Megf10 deficiency showing impaired satellite cell migration and impaired muscle regeneration. It adds functional and animal-model evidence for MEGF10 myopathy but reports no patients.

findings.statement: Li et al. (2021) cultured single myofibers isolated from the extensor digitorum longus muscles of Megf10-null mice and wildtype mice. At 24, 48, and 72 hours, fewer satellite cells had detached from Megf10-null myofibers than from wildtype myofibers. The authors concluded that Megf10 deficiency is associated with impaired satellite cell activation and migration.
quotes: At each time point, fewer satellite cells were detached from Megf10−/− live myofibers than from wild‐type live myofibers, indicating that Megf10 deficiency is associated with impaired satellite cell activation and migration.
Individual myofibers were isolated from the extensor digitorum longus (EDL) muscles of 6 Megf10−/− and 5 wild‐type mice according to a standard protocol [23].

findings.statement: Li et al. (2021) found fewer Pax7+/MyoD+ activated satellite cells associated with Megf10-null myofibers than with wildtype myofibers, and these cells migrated shorter distances. Satellite cells detached from Megf10-null myofibers also had fewer MyoD-positive nuclei. The authors concluded that Megf10 contributes to an early stage of satellite cell activation, during which the cells migrate to target myofibers.
quotes: Manual counts of attached and detached Pax7+/MyoD+ cells showed that these cells were less abundant for Megf10−/− myofibers compared to wild‐type myofibers (Fig. 2B).

Satellite cells detached from myofibers were cultured separately, showing less abundant MyoD expression among DAPI‐positive nuclei of Megf10−/− satellite cells compared to wild‐type satellite cells (Fig. 2D,E).

Our current data show that Megf10 deficiency impairs migration of Pax7+/MyoD+ activated satellite cells and is associated with reduced numbers of MyoD + cells, providing further evidence that Megf10 contributes to an early stage of satellite cell activation during which the cells migrate to target myofibers.

findings.statement: Li et al. (2021) injured the tibialis anterior muscle of Megf10-null and wildtype mice with 3 sequential intramuscular barium chloride injections, starting at 2 months of age, to deplete the satellite cell pool. Compared with wildtype muscle, injured Megf10-null muscle showed significantly reduced regeneration, with pockets of atrophic fibers, clusters of small myofibers with internalized nuclei, and greater variability in fiber size. Fibronectin staining showed more fibrosis in injured Megf10-null muscle.
quotes: Hematoxylin and eosin staining of representative sections from the injected muscles revealed significantly reduced regeneration potential with pronounced pockets of atrophic fibers and greater overall fiber size variability in Megf10−/− tibialis anterior muscles injected with barium chloride compared to wild‐type tibialis anterior muscles (Fig. 3B).
Greater densities of fibronectin were measured via ImageJ quantification in Megf10−/− muscles compared to wild‐type muscles (Fig. 3C).

findings.statement: Li et al. (2021) suggested that impaired satellite cell function and impaired muscle regeneration caused by MEGF10 deficiency could help explain why the clinical manifestations of MEGF10 myopathy persist. They noted that muscle function generally does not improve in affected patients.
quotes: This information could help explain the persistent nature of the clinical manifestations of MEGF10 myopathy, as muscle function generally does not improve in human patients affected by this disease [1, 2].
Megf10 deficiency is associated with impaired muscle regeneration, due in part to defects in satellite cell function.

relevance_reason: Abstract reports the discovery of MEGF10 mutations as the cause of early-onset myopathy, areflexia, respiratory distress and dysphagia (EMARDD), the severe allelic form. This gives gene-level context for the mild variant entry. The abstract does not describe mild-variant patients or specific variants.

findings.statement: Logan et al. (2011) used phased haplotype analysis followed by targeted exome sequencing to identify mutations in the MEGF10 gene in patients with a previously unrecognized type of infantile myopathy. They named it early-onset myopathy, areflexia, respiratory distress and dysphagia (EMARDD).
quotes: We used phased haplotype analysis with subsequent targeted exome sequencing to identify MEGF10 mutations in a previously unidentified type of infantile myopathy with diaphragmatic weakness, areflexia, respiratory distress and dysphagia.

findings.statement: Logan et al. (2011) described an infantile myopathy with diaphragmatic weakness, areflexia, respiratory distress and dysphagia. They noted that infantile myopathies with diaphragmatic paralysis are genetically heterogeneous and that clinical symptoms do not help distinguish between them.
quotes: Infantile myopathies with diaphragmatic paralysis are genetically heterogeneous, and clinical symptoms do not assist in differentiating between them.
a previously unidentified type of infantile myopathy with diaphragmatic weakness, areflexia, respiratory distress and dysphagia

findings.statement: Logan et al. (2011) reported that MEGF10 is highly expressed in activated satellite cells and regulates their proliferation, differentiation, and fusion into multinucleated myofibers. These processes are greatly reduced in muscle from individuals with EMARDD.
quotes: MEGF10 is highly expressed in activated satellite cells and regulates their proliferation as well as their differentiation and fusion into multinucleated myofibers, which are greatly reduced in muscle from individuals with early onset myopathy, areflexia, respiratory distress and dysphagia.

relevance_reason: Preclinical therapeutic and animal/cellular model study of MEGF10 myopathy (SSRIs). It is relevant to the MEGF10 disorder spectrum, but the abstract does not single out the mild variant.

findings.statement: Saha et al. (2019) ran a small-molecule screen in Megf10-deficient myoblasts and identified 2 selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), sertraline and escitalopram. Follow-up testing in Megf10 -/- mouse myoblasts, induced pluripotent stem cell-derived myoblasts from patients with MEGF10 myopathy, Drosophila deficient in the MEGF10 homolog Drpr, and megf10 mutant zebrafish showed that sertraline was highly effective at relieving abnormalities in all of these models and restored Notch1 deficiencies. The authors concluded that SSRIs, especially sertraline, show promise as therapies for MEGF10 myopathy and suggested that the mechanism may involve the Notch pathway.
quotes: Secondary evaluations were performed on primary screen hits using myoblasts derived from Megf10-/- mice, induced pluripotent stem cell-derived myoblasts from MEGF10 myopathy patients, mutant Drosophila that are deficient in the homologue of MEGF10 (Drpr) and megf10 mutant zebrafish.

In depth follow-up analyses demonstrated that sertraline was highly effective in alleviating abnormalities across multiple models of the disease including mouse myoblast, human myoblast, Drosophila and zebrafish models.
Sertraline also restored deficiencies of Notch1 in disease models.

relevance_reason: Functional study of the C326R and C774R MEGF10 missense mutations from the mild-phenotype family. Phosphorylation defects line up with the genotype-phenotype correlation (C326R milder), and the work points to a pathogenic mechanism.

findings.statement: Mitsuhashi et al. (2013) noted that a family with a milder phenotype carried compound heterozygous missense mutations C326R and C774R in MEGF10. The 3 affected individuals were in their third decade, one was still ambulatory, and they needed only noninvasive nocturnal ventilatory support. C774R paired with a nonsense mutation had been seen in a severely affected family. The authors suggested that C774R is as deleterious as a nonsense mutation, while C326R may be less consequential.
quotes: Later, we reported a sixth family with a milder phenotype who harbored the compound heterozygous missense mutations C326R and C774R, located at the second cysteine of the 6th EGF-like domain and the 4th cysteine of the 16th EGF-like domain, respectively.

The three affected individuals in this family are now in their third decade, and one is still ambulatory. They have milder respiratory complications than the initial cohort of 5 families, only requiring non-invasive nocturnal ventilatory support.
These observations suggest that the C774R mutation is as deleterious as a nonsense mutation, while the C326R mutation may be less consequential.

phenotypes.text: nocturnal hypoventilation requiring noninvasive ventilatory support

findings.statement: Mitsuhashi et al. (2013) found that MEGF10 C326R and C774R mutants overexpressed in HEK293T and C2C12 cells showed reduced tyrosine phosphorylation. The reduction was severe for C774R and mild for C326R. Neither mutation changed subcellular localization. C774R showed reduced N-glycosylation and weaker c-Src binding and phosphorylation. The authors noted that these patterns are consistent with the genotype-phenotype correlation in the human disease.
quotes: Tyrosine phosphorylation was severely decreased in the C774R mutant and mildly decreased in the C326R mutant (Fig. 1B, Supplementary Fig. 1A).

Mutant C326R and C774R MEGF10 display the same subcellular localization patterns as wild type MEGF10 in both HEK293T and C2C12 cells, suggesting that the phosphorylation defects of these mutant MEGF10 proteins is not due to aberrant subcellular localization
In addition, tyrosine phosphorylation of C326R and C774R MEGF10 mutant proteins was reduced in patterns that are consistent with observations of genotype-phenotype correlations in the human disease.

findings.statement: Mitsuhashi et al. (2013) identified Y1030 as the major tyrosine phosphorylation site of MEGF10 and showed that it is phosphorylated at least in part by c-Src, which co-immunoprecipitated with MEGF10. Overexpressing wild-type MEGF10 or the phosphomimetic Y1030D mutant increased C2C12 myoblast proliferation, but the Y1030F mutant did not.
quotes: Among these, only the Y1030F mutant lost tyrosine phosphorylation, suggesting that Y1030 is a major tyrosine phosphorylation site for MEGF10 (Fig. 2B).
These results indicate that overexpressed MEGF10 is phosphorylated by c-Src.

A cell viability assay and a proliferation marker Ki-67 positive cell count confirmed that overexpression of wild type MEGF10 and the Y1030D mutant increases cell proliferation in C2C12 myoblasts, whereas the overexpressed Y1030F mutant did not

findings.statement: Mitsuhashi et al. (2013) suggested that MEGF10 myopathy may be caused by a defect in muscle satellite cell proliferation resulting from impaired MEGF10 tyrosine phosphorylation signaling. They also suggested that the 16th EGF-like domain may matter more for signaling than the 6th.
quotes: These results suggest that MEGF10 myopathy may be caused by a defect in muscle satellite cell proliferation due to impaired MEGF10 tyrosine phosphorylation signaling.

C326R results in a milder effect both biochemically and clinically than C774R, suggesting that the 16th EGF-like domain may be more important for recognizing extracellular stimuli and conducting signals than the 6th EGF-like domain.
